paper.title: Predicting Privileged Information Effectiveness for On-Policy Self-Distillation
paper.author_block: Kaijian Zou Affiliation: University of Michigan – Ann Arbor Emiliano Penaloza Affiliation: Mila MohammadHossein Rezaei Affiliation: Scale AI Anisha Gunjal Affiliation: Scale AI Mohit Raghavendra Affiliation: Scale AI Lu Wang Affiliation: University of Michigan – Ann Arbor Yunzhong He Affiliation: Scale AI Anas Mahmoud Affiliation: Scale AI
paper.abstract:
Abstract On-policy self-distillation ( OPSD ) enables large language models (LLMs) to
learn from privileged information ( PI ) without a separate teacher
model. However, prior work largely treats PI as a fixed design choice, leaving
the effects of its content and construction poorly understood. This challenge
is particularly important in multi-turn agentic settings, where trajectories
contain actions, observations, and reasoning that can be transformed into PI
in many ways. We systematically evaluate 16 PI configurations across three
multi-turn agentic benchmarks and three student models that vary in scale and
reasoning mode. We find that PI effectiveness depends on its content,
generation source, and the student model. Information-dense trajectories and
PI produced by more capable generators generally yield larger gains, whereas
thinking models benefit less consistently. To assess PI before training, we
compare PI utility with two KL-based metrics: sampled-token reverse KL ( D D ) and
error-step KL contrast ( Δ ​ d err − \Delta d^{-}_{\mathrm{err}} ). The KL-based metrics track post-training performance
more consistently than PI utility, which can be distorted by information
leakage. Empirically, selecting each task’s PI by Δ ​ d err − \Delta d^{-}_{\mathrm{err}} also
improves post-training performance over random selection, most when the
PI candidates differ widely. Finally, effective PI remains beneficial when combined with GRPO,
allowing the combined objective to outperform a strong GRPO baseline. Overall,

paper.title: Distill Until Divergence: Error-Truncated Hindsight Distillation for Agentic RL
paper.author_block: Yibin Huang Affiliation: Faculty of Computing, Harbin Institute of Technology Conghui Zhu † † thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Faculty of Computing, Harbin Institute of Technology
paper.abstract: Abstract Long-horizon interaction requires agents to make multiple decisions in a changing environment. Outcome-based GRPO lacks fine-grained guidance for intermediate decisions. Recent methods distill completed trajectories into reusable skills and use hindsight-conditioned OPD to provide dense token-level credit. However, skill-induced probability shifts do not necessarily represent reward-aligned credit; especially after an erroneous action changes subsequent interaction states, skill-conditioned supervision may become mismatched with the current state. To address this mismatch, we propose ETRO, which routes two complementary hindsight skills according to trajectory outcomes and error boundaries: Positive skills capture successful workflows to reinforce successful trajectories and pre-error decisions, while Negative skills capture failure-specific corrections to target decisive errors. The post-error suffix is optimized exclusively by GRPO, retaining outcome-based learning without extending potentially mismatched hindsight supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate competitive task performance and support effective fine-grained credit allocation.

paper.title: ToolOPD: Credit-Aware On-Policy Distillation for Tool-Use Agents
paper.author_block: Chu Zhao Affiliation: Northeastern University Lei Tang Affiliation: Honor Device Co., Ltd Yanming Wang Affiliation: Honor Device Co., Ltd Jianzhe Zhao Affiliation: Northeastern University Guibing Guo † † thanks: Corresponding authors. Affiliation: Northeastern University Zhengzong Chen Yuanyuan Zhao Affiliation: Honor Device Co., Ltd Fei Huang Affiliation: Honor Device Co., Ltd
paper.abstract:
Abstract On-policy distillation (OPD) enhances the capabilities of small language agents by providing dense, token-level supervision from a teacher model on student-generated trajectories. However, standard OPD implicitly assumes that credit is uniformly distributed across long-horizon trajectories, assigning the same strength of teacher supervision to different actions. Through credit-distribution analysis and outcome-reversal counterfactual experiments, we find that trajectory credit is concentrated on a small number of critical actions. Moreover, even when the trajectory is held fixed, reversing only the final outcome substantially changes the credit assigned to multiple interaction turns. These findings show that the uniform-credit assumption fails to identify critical decisions and ultimately degrades the model’s reasoning accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose ToolOPD , an outcome-aware on-policy distillation framework designed for long-horizon tool use. ToolOPD first summarizes each completed trajectory and
its outcome into a reusable hindsight skill. It then measures how this skill changes the teacher’s probability of each student action token and converts the change into outcome-aware credit. The resulting credit preserves supervision that supports successful decisions or discourages failed ones, while suppressing irrelevant and conflicting signals. ToolOPD uses these credits to reweight the action-level distillation loss and jointly optimizes it with reinforcement learning. paper.title: Self-Evolving Agents through Privileged Retrospective Distillation
paper.author_block:
Yuhang Zhou       
Yifan Wu       
Bo Peng       
Mingyi Wang       
Jiayi Liu Xiangjun Fan       
Lizhu Zhang      
Zhuokai Zhao Meta AI {zyhang, zhuokai}@meta.com
paper.abstract:
Abstract Self-evolving agents aim to improve from their own experience rather than remaining fixed once deployed.
In practice, however, naturally collected agent trajectories often lack ground-truth solutions or verifier-derived rewards, making them difficult to learn from.
We observe that these trajectories become substantially more informative in retrospect .
When the agent takes an action, it knows only what has happened so far, but looking back after the trajectory ends, the same action can be judged with knowledge the agent lacked at that moment, including how the environment responded afterward and how related tasks in its accumulated experience succeeded or failed.
Based on this observation, we introduce Retrospective Self-Distillation ( RSD ) , a multi-round self-evolution framework
in which the same model, given privileged retrospective context built from its own experience, acts as a teacher that re-scores its own actions, and the resulting distribution is distilled back into the policy through on-policy self-distillation.
The privileged context combines cross-task precedents and lessons with turn-level reflection and future hindsight, allowing both successful and imperfect trajectories to provide dense supervision. RSD is also built to make this supervision improve alongside the agent.
Every round, precedents and lessons are re-derived from the experience bank enlarged with the current policy’s trajectories, and reflection and hindsight are computed fresh for each new trajectory, so the teacher always scores the policy against its most recent experience.

paper.title: MMSearch-OPD: Easy Made Hard, Hard Made Learnable for Long-Horizon Multimodal Search Agents
paper.author_block: Huanyao Zhang 1 * ‡ \ddagger Jiepeng Zhou 2 * Jiaye Lin 3 * Ontai Tang 4 Jingtian Hao 1 Mugeng Liu 1 Ru Peng 5 Lang Mei 6 Xiaohan Yu 6 Liyan Liu 6 Chong Chen 6 † \dagger Wentao Zhang 1 † \dagger 1 Peking University 2 HKUST(GZ) 3 Tsinghua University 4 The University of Hong Kong 5 Zhejiang University 6 Huawei Cloud BU * Equal contribution ‡ \ddagger Project Leader † \dagger Corresponding authors
paper.abstract:
Abstract Multimodal deep search is moving from short queries to long-horizon
investigations that continually acquire evidence. However, training
such agents remains constrained by limited challenging training
questions and insufficient process feedback.
We introduce MMSearch-OPD , combining controllable data
refinement with joint reinforcement learning (RL) and on-policy
distillation (OPD). Our Refine pipeline performs targeted
expansion of reasoning chains derived from existing simple
multimodal questions. Parameterized transformations control
search depth and cross-modal evidence requirements while reusing
existing image–question pairs. For training, answer rewards and
lightweight behavior penalties guide RL, while the reward gap
modulates token-level teacher guidance on imperfect student
trajectories. An exponentially decaying distillation coefficient
reduces teacher dependence as training proceeds.
Experiments show gains from data refinement and further
improvements from joint training after SFT, indicating stronger
long-horizon multimodal deep search capabilities.

paper.title: Tree-Aware Posterior Distillation for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
paper.author_block: Heming Zou 1,2,* Qi Wang 1 Yixiu Mao 1 Yun Qu 1 Yuyi Guo 1,2,* Zeyuan Liu 1,2,* Affiliation: Chenglin Li 1 , Weijie Liu 2 , Saiyong Yang 2 , Xiangyang Ji 1
paper.abstract: Abstract Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a scalable post-training paradigm for large language models. However, training agents over long-horizon interactions presents two challenges: using only terminal rewards makes turn-level credit assignment sparse and high-variance, while sequential mini-batch updates on a fixed rollout batch introduce policy staleness as the current policy drifts from the behavior policy. Existing approaches obtain denser credit via learned critics, process reward models, or on-policy distillation, but they rely on a value network, step-level annotations, or a stronger external teacher that increase training complexity. Meanwhile, importance sampling and clipping mitigate policy drift, but they do not specify a finite target that stops sequential updates from overshooting. In this work, we introduce TreeOPSD, a critic-free, tree-aware posterior self-distillation framework for long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning. Treating each interaction turn as a tree node, TreeOPSD branches alternative continuations from shared prefixes and recursively backs up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit. It then maps each credit to a closed-form, bounded teacher distribution parameterized by the likelihood ratio relative to the frozen behavior policy. Minimizing the divergence between this teacher and the student policy recovers the policy-gradient direction as the tangent at the behavior policy while bounding updates toward a finite target across sequential mini-batches. paper.title: Elicitation or Expansion? Demystifying Gains from Agent Harness Optimization
paper.author_block:
Younghyun Kim  ,
Wooseok Seo,
Minseo Kim,
Seunghyuk Oh,
Minjae Lee Donghoon Kim,
Hyung Il Koo,
Jaehyung Kim,
Wonjun Kang FuriosaAI Yonsei University University of California, Berkeley Project page: furiosa-air.github.io/elicitation-or-expansion Code: github.com/furiosa-ai/elicitation-or-expansion Dataset: datasets/furiosa-ai/elicitation-or-expansion-trajectories † † thanks: Equal contribution. ^ † ^{\dagger} Co-corresponding authors.
paper.abstract:
Abstract Recent studies in harness optimization have shown substantial performance gains in language model agents without updating model weights.
A well-designed harness more effectively leverages the underlying model’s capabilities by shaping context, tool use, and execution workflows.
However, naïve success rates alone do not fully characterize whether optimized harness yields more reliable success on tasks already within reach ( elicitation ) or a broader range of solvable tasks ( expansion ).
This distinction is crucial for recursive self-improvement and evolutionary search, as expansion may provide a broader range of successful experiences to push the capability boundaries.
Despite the growing significance, this distinction remains underexplored in harness optimization.
We conduct a systematic analysis to study the effect of gains from harness optimization.
Building on pass ​ @ ​ k \mathrm{pass@}k analyses in the reinforcement learning (RL) literature that compare models before and after RL training, we compare optimized harnesses with their pre-optimization counterparts.
Specifically, we assess changes in reachable task coverage, compare harness optimization with model scaling and increased inference-time compute, and examine how gains vary with task difficulty.
Across static prediction and dynamic tasks, we find that pass ​ @ ​ 1 \mathrm{pass@}1 advantages of harness over stronger interventions can reverse at larger attempt budgets and aggregate gains conceal shortfalls on hard tasks, underscoring the need for a fine-grained diagnosis.

paper.title: Productive State-Space Exploration for Multi-turn RL in LLM Agents
paper.author_block: Mohammed Haroon Dupty † Affiliation: Institute of Advanced Computing Affiliation: and Intelligence, A*STAR Email: haroon@u.nus.edu Yong Liang Goh Affiliation: Grabtaxi Holdings Pte Ltd Email: gyl@u.nus.edu Song Guo Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Affiliation: Science and Technology Email: songguo@cse.ust.hk Wee Sun Lee Affiliation: School of Computing, Affiliation: National University of Singapore Email: leews@comp.nus.edu.sg
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement Learning (RL) for Large Language Model (LLM) agents in multi-turn, long-horizon environments remains challenging due to inefficient action selection and repetitive behavioral patterns. In particular, agents often become trapped in high-confidence yet unproductive behaviors, repeatedly executing invalid actions or entering action loops that hinder task completion. We observe that these frequently violate environment preconditions, revealing a mismatch between the agent’s representation of the internal state and the dynamics of the underlying environment. In addition, repetitive high-confidence actions lead to cyclical behaviors that provide little to no progress towards the goal.
We argue that addressing these challenges requires more productive task-aligned exploration to improve the agent’s understanding of environment dynamics. Motivated by intrinsic curiosity-driven exploration, we propose a conditional state-space exploration framework that balances task completion with intrinsic information-seeking behavior. Specifically, we introduce an intrinsic reward that penalizes actions whose observation duplicates prior state memory. This provides the benefit of reducing redundant behaviors and encouraging state-space coverage without relying on a general information-theoretic measure. Strong experimental results demonstrate that our approach substantially improves policy learning in multi-turn environments, mitigating invalid actions and repetitive loops.

paper.title:
Grounded Credit Assignment in Reinforcement Learning
for Multi-Turn Search Agents
paper.author_block: Qirui Liu 1* , Hao Chen 2*† , Yi Wen 3 , Weijie Shi 4 , Yao Zhao 5 , Xianhe Chen 6 , Hao Zhao 2 , Xing Tang 7 , Weihong Luo 2 , Yuyu Luo 8† 1 South China University of Technology, 2 FiT, Tencent, 3 City University of Hong Kong, 4 The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, 5 Nanjing University, 6 Imperial College London, 7 Shenzhen Technology University, 8 The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) * Equal contribution. † Corresponding authors.
paper.abstract:
Abstract Outcome-reward reinforcement learning such as GRPO gives every token of a search-agent rollout the same advantage, although the rollout exercises two capabilities: finding evidence and using it.
We show that accuracy improves without grounding: Search-R1 raises accuracy on all seven QA benchmarks, yet on Bamboogle the evidence-supported share of correct answers falls from 84.0% to 42.9%.
We attribute this to GRPO’s credit assignment: rollouts that retrieve answer-bearing evidence are favoured in aggregate only in proportion to their accuracy gain over the rest, a grounding gap that answering from memory or misusing evidence shrinks or reverses.
To address this, we propose Grounded Credit Assignment (GCA 1 1 1 Code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Grounded-Credit-Assignment-6320 ), which uses verifiable sub-outcomes (evidence retrieval and answer correctness) to correct search and answer credit separately: a wrong answer is blamed more than the search that found the evidence, and a correct answer that bypasses retrievable evidence is credited less.
Never negative on evidence-finding search, the correction does not shrink with the grounding gap; capped at 10% of each token’s advantage, it never overrides the outcome signal.
Without extra models, rollouts, or training stages, GCA improves average EM over Search-R1 by 5.7 (Qwen2.5-3B) and 6.3 points (Qwen3-30B-A3B) and raises this share from 76.9% to 93.4%.

paper.title: EG-GRPO: Evidence-Guided Step-level Credit Assignment for Deep Search Agents
paper.author_block: Sijia Luo Affiliation: Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China Affiliation: Key Laboratory of Data Engineering and Knowledge Engineering, MOE, China Affiliation: Ant Group, Beijing, China Email: sijialuo23@gmail.com Mengjie Gao Affiliation: Ant Group, Beijing, China Email: liuxiao.gmj@antgroup.com Yuxiao He Affiliation: Ant Group, Beijing, China Email: matthew.hyx@antgroup.com Mengshu Sun Affiliation: Ant Group, Beijing, China Email: mengshu.sms@antgroup.com Cuiping Li Affiliation: Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China Affiliation: Beijing Key Laboratory of Intelligent Database Systems and Applications, China Email: licuiping@ruc.edu.cn Hong Chen Affiliation: Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China Affiliation: Engineering Research Center of Database and Business Intelligence, MOE, China Email: chong@ruc.edu.cn Jing Zhang † † thanks: Corresponding Author. Affiliation: Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China Affiliation: Key Laboratory of Data Engineering and Knowledge Engineering, MOE, China Email: zhang-jing@ruc.edu.cn
paper.abstract: Abstract LLM-based search agents demonstrate strong capabilities in long-horizon information seeking and reasoning, typically trained via reinforcement learning. However, existing approaches predominantly rely on trajectory-level outcome rewards, providing limited supervision for complex search and reasoning processes. Although step-level credit assignment offers a promising solution, obtaining reliable and task-grounded supervision for open-ended search remains challenging. In this paper, we propose E vidence- G uided G roup R elative P olicy O ptimization ( EG-GRPO ), a framework that derives step-level supervision from the evidence annotations available in synthetic deep search data. EG-GRPO identifies the first supporting citation for each required evidence claim and uses the newly acquired evidence to construct step-level process rewards. By representing the accumulated evidence as an evolving knowledge state, EG-GRPO further performs state-conditioned relative advantage estimation and combines the resulting step-level signal with the standard trajectory-level outcome advantage. Experiments on five challenging deep search benchmarks show that EG-GRPO generally outperforms standard GRPO and existing reward-enhanced and step-level RL baselines across different model scales. These results demonstrate that task-grounded evidence annotations can provide effective process supervision for credit assignment in deep search RL.

paper.title: Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation for Agentic Knowledge Graph Question Answering
paper.author_block: Mingyuan Li Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Novel Software Technology,Nanjing University, Nanjing, China Yucheng Li Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Novel Software Technology,Nanjing University, Nanjing, China Xiaxia Wang Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Oxford * Corresponding author: gcheng@nju.edu.cn Gong Cheng Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Novel Software Technology,Nanjing University, Nanjing, China
paper.abstract: Abstract Agentic knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) requires large language models (LLMs) to solve complex questions through multi-turn interactions with a knowledge graph (KG). Outcome-supervised reinforcement learning derives verifiable outcome rewards from final answers but uniformly assigns each rollout’s outcome-level advantage to all policy-generated tokens, creating a trajectory-to-operation mismatch since KG operations within a rollout can have varying effects on the search process and final answer. To address this, we propose Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation (OACR), which employs a training-only KG-state outcome model to estimate outcome-reward changes between adjacent KG search states and converts them into operation credit, from which token-wise weights are derived. These multiplicative weights reallocate token-level update magnitudes while preserving the sign of the outcome-level advantage at every generated token. Across three benchmarks, OACR achieves stronger overall performance than existing KGQA methods while using fewer inference-time LLM calls and tokens.

paper.title: Self-Credit : Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling
paper.author_block: Fangcong Yin Affiliation: Meta Ming Yin Affiliation: Meta Affiliation: Duke University Tanvi Bhandarkar Affiliation: Meta Aashu Singh Affiliation: Meta Eryk Helenowski Affiliation: Meta Shlok Kumar Mishra Affiliation: Meta Saghar Hosseini Affiliation: Meta Karthik Abinav Sankararaman Affiliation: Meta Greg Durrett Affiliation: New York University Dinkar Juyal Affiliation: Meta
paper.abstract: Abstract LLM agents are commonly trained with RLVR, but the sparse nature of typical RLVR rewards makes credit assignment challenging, especially for long-horizon tasks. We propose Self-Credit , an end-to-end agentic RL method that creates dense supervision signals from sparse outcome rewards using self-generated credit assignment via intra-group rescaling . Self-Credit builds on group-based RL with three components. First, during its rollouts, the policy model generates summaries with citations to earlier turns containing critical evidence, which serve as self-generated credit. Second, we refine this model-generated credit with intra-group rescaling , which compares cited actions across successful and failed rollouts for the same prompt. This approach uses group-level agreement and disagreement to remove undeserved credit and further emphasize credit assigned to critical actions. Third, advantage reweighting uses the rescaled credit weights to update the advantages of the cited turns. On BrowseComp-Plus, Self-Credit improves over the base models by 37.0 37.0 and 36.2 36.2 points on Qwen3 8B and 32B respectively, and outperforms the strongest agentic RL baselines by 8.5 8.5 and 5.6 5.6 points, respectively. Self-Credit also improves over the strongest baselines by 4.9 4.9 points on GAIA and 4.7 4.7 points on xBench-DeepSearch. Analyses show that self-generated credit provides useful signals for selecting critical actions, and that intra-group rescaling, especially on failed rollouts, is important across model scales.

paper.title: FALCA: Falsification-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Hierarchical Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Deep Search Agents
paper.author_block: Zijun Dou Kun Luo Chaofan Li Shuqi Lu Zheng Liu \corresponding
paper.abstract: Abstract Long-horizon deep search requires LLM agents to iteratively decompose complex information needs, gather evidence from external sources, and maintain a reliable research state under multiple constraints. A central challenge is that early mistakes can be amplified over the search trajectory: agents may anchor on an incorrect candidate, collect partially supporting evidence, overlook contradictions, and accumulate errors that misguide subsequent reasoning. We propose FALCA , a falsification-aware framework that formulates deep search as a propose–falsify process. FALCA adopts a collaborative Searcher–Falsifier architecture, where the Searcher proposes candidate answers or sub-answers, while independent Falsifiers actively seek counterevidence, check unmet constraints, identify conflicts, and produce concise falsification reports for research-state revision. To strengthen this loop, we introduce falsification-aware training, combining SFT warmup on falsification trajectories with agentic RL based on parallel rollouts and hierarchical credit assignment over research stages, state transitions, and actions. Experiments on five search benchmarks show that FALCA improves long-horizon deep search performance over backbone and harness ablations, while reducing confirmation bias and error accumulation through more effective falsification and research-state revision.

paper.title: From Outcomes to Steps: Reliable Success-Aware Critic Learning for Long-Horizon Language Agents
paper.author_block: Jiaxi Liu Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University Shixiong Kai Affiliation: Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab Zhentao Tang Affiliation: Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab Yang Li Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University Yuqi Cui Affiliation: Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab Mingxuan Yuan Affiliation: Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab Junchi Yan Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement learning for long-horizon language agents requires identifying whether intermediate actions make eventual task success more or less likely when supervision is available only at trajectory level.
The main difficulty is that a critic with aggregate return-prediction accuracy may still fail to resolve the local value differences needed to assign credit to actions , especially under sparse feedback and function approximation. Conventional critics estimate future return, but policy improvement also depends on knowing whether each intermediate decision makes task success more or less likely.
We introduce SCALE , an actor–critic framework that augments conventional return estimation with explicit prediction of eventual task success. At each interaction prefix, the critic predicts a return value and a Success Value , defined as the probability that the task will eventually be completed from that prefix. SCALE converts changes in Success Value into multi-step action credit through Success-GAE and modulates its contribution according to the estimated reliability of the predictor, while retaining the token-level PPO objective.
Across five agent benchmarks and three model backbones, SCALE improves task performance over the compared RL baselines in most settings, with gains of up to 4.1 percentage points in success rate. Separate critic-learning analyses show that SCALE also improves critic estimation and training stability.

paper.title: CoworkEnv: Synthesizing Training Environments for Long-Horizon Cowork Agents
paper.author_block:
Zhongwei XIE Yiming DU Jiaxin BAI Baixuan XU Chunyang LI Xiyu REN Wei FAN Tianshi ZHENG Weizhi DU Jingqiao YU Xingsu LI Zhaowei WANG Yangqiu SONG
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology The Chinese University of Hong Kong Hong Kong Baptist University Independent Researcher {zxiebk, zwanggy}@connect.ust.hk ydu@se.cuhk.edu.hk yqsong@ust.hk * Corresponding author: zwanggy@connect.ust.hk
paper.abstract: Abstract AI coworkers must coordinate tools, communicate across turns, and act on changing workspace state while respecting workflow constraints. Constructing training experience for these capabilities requires coherent requests, service records, tool interfaces, and grading checks. We present CoworkEnv , a capability-guided framework for synthesizing executable training environments for AI coworkers. Workflow requirements guide task construction, and programmatic validation with feedback repair checks generated specifications and grading behavior. Teacher executions yield curated demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while student interactions provide rollouts and rewards for reinforcement learning (RL). Using these resources, we train compact PocketWorker models. For Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, SFT raises the mean score from 46.6 to 64.1 on Claw-Eval, including a 31.9-point gain on Multi-turn tasks. An SFT-only extension to ClawMark demonstrates applicability across coworker benchmarks. We further compare RL training dynamics across configurations that vary reward processing and credit assignment. Improving training rewards provide preliminary evidence that the constructed environments support policy optimization.

paper.title: VeriCUA: Learning Proactive Verification for Reliable GUI Agent Rewards
paper.author_block: Zhizhou Wang † † thanks: Equal contribution ( jenojeff66@gmail.com , lyx23@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn ). Affiliation: Southwest Jiaotong University Yaxi Lu 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Tsinghua University Zhong Zhang † † thanks: Corresponding author ( zhong.zhang@uestc.edu.cn , fangminghk@gmail.com ). Affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China Zikun Hu Affiliation: National University of Singapore Xin Cong Affiliation: Tsinghua University Yankai Lin Affiliation: Renmin University of China Fangming Liu 2 2 footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: Peng Cheng Laboratory
paper.abstract: Abstract Reinforcement learning for computer-use agents increasingly relies on proactive reward agents that interact with the post-execution GUI environment to verify what recorded screenshots cannot reveal. The reliability of such verification hinges on two coupled decisions: what to check and when to stop. Existing methods leave these decisions to prompted foundation models. However, neither scaling up the model nor providing few-shot examples reliably improves verification: prompted Judges ranging from 4B to GPT-5.4 all plateau at 68 % 68\% – 70 % 70\% macro-average agreement. This is because the value of a check depends on the environment rather than the task alone, and becomes apparent only through execution. Learning from execution is itself constrained, as the Actor’s terminal state cannot be faithfully replicated during training, allowing only one verification attempt per state. We introduce VeriCUA , a proactive reward agent that learns its verification strategy from these single attempts. A trainable Judge decides what to check and when to stop, while a frozen Probe executes the checks in the live environment. Online reinforcement learning optimizes the Judge for both verdict correctness and efficient Probe use, with returns normalized across terminal states. Trained only on OSWorld and evaluated without further training on MobileWorld and WebArena-Verified, VeriCUA achieves the highest reward agreement across all three benchmarks and lies on the agreement–cost Pareto frontier among proactive verifiers. It surpasses few-shot GPT-5.4 by 5.36 5.36 points with 47.6 %

paper.title: Specification Gaming and a Constrained Reinforcement Learning Mitigation in a Cleaning Gridworld
paper.author_block: Hilda Adwubi Osei Affiliation: Department of Industrial Engineering Affiliation: Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology Affiliation: Kumasi, Ghana Email: hildaosei109@gmail.com
paper.abstract: Abstract Reinforcement learning agents optimize exactly the reward signal they are given, which can diverge sharply from an intended true objective when that signal is only a proxy for it; this failure mode is known as specification gaming. Existing evidence for this failure mode is largely observational, with comparatively few demonstrations pairing a controlled, deliberately constructed proxy/true gap with a mitigation that carries a verifiable guarantee rather than only an empirical improvement. We construct a minimal gridworld in which a cleaning-robot agent can either genuinely remove dirt or conceal it from a cheap sensor, and show that a standard deep Q-network trained only on the sensor’s proxy reward converges to a policy that games it completely, reaching near-maximal proxy reward while never achieving the true objective. We then introduce a constrained reinforcement learning fix, penalizing the specific behaviors through which the agent exploits the gap, and show that it eliminates the gaming behavior from the final policy while substantially recovering true-objective performance. We further derive and empirically verify an exact accounting identity relating the proxy reward, true reward, and our cost signal for this environment, showing that the cost signal measures the proxy/true gap exactly rather than merely tracking it, and yields a deterministic guarantee under a hard-constrained variant of the method.

paper.title: Training the Whole Agent, Not Just the Model
paper.author_block: Lingxiao Tang Wei Tao Yiwen Guo Lingfeng Bao Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [
paper.abstract: Abstract Training coding agents typically updates the policy while keeping the harness fixed. During training, trajectories reveal flawed repair strategies and interaction problems that vary across tasks and change as the policy learns. We introduce HarnessAdapt-RL, which trains the policy and adapts its harness during reinforcement learning. For flawed repair strategies, a frozen teacher generates task-specific mechanism-level skills. For interaction problems recurring across tasks, a separate teacher model evolves tools and hooks, keeping each change only if it improves the observed pass rate or the observed trainable rate without lowering either. The policy trains with the adapted harness, and its new trajectories guide further adaptation. With a 9B base model, HarnessAdapt-RL improves pass@1 over GRPO by 9.8, 12.6, and 6.4 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual, and Pro, and outperforms GRPO with the human-designed OpenHands harness. Gains from mechanism-level skills persist after their removal at evaluation. Re-evolving tools and hooks as the policy changes outperforms freezing early versions. Removing them at deployment, in contrast, costs up to 7.7 percentage points. Training therefore produces a model–harness pair: the trained policy and the evolved tools and hooks, with skills removed at deployment.

paper.title: Mosaic : Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning
paper.author_block: Yilong Xu Affiliation: LARK, HKUST(GZ) Minrui Xu Affiliation: LARK, HKUST(GZ) Xinyu Zhou Affiliation: LARK, HKUST(GZ) Xiang Long, Haochen Tan Affiliation: Foundation Model Lab, Huawei Zhijiang Guo Corresponding author: Zhijiang Guo (zhijiangguo@hkust-gz.edu.cn), Haochen Tan (haochetan2-c@my.cityu.edu.hk) Affiliation: LARK, HKUST(GZ) Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong Affiliation: HKUST
paper.abstract: Abstract Most existing agentic reinforcement learning methods assume single-session trajectories, where interaction proceeds within one continuously accumulated context. However, agentic techniques such as context compaction and subagent forking may produce trajectories spanning multiple sessions, creating a mismatch between the single-session training assumption and inference-time execution. Therefore, we introduce Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning , a more general setting that supports an arbitrary number of sessions within a trajectory. Under this setting, a widely adopted method is to broadcast trajectory-level advantages to all sessions, but this does not distinguish contributions from various sessions or guide session allocation within trajectories. To address this issue, we propose Mosaic , a multi-session agentic RL method with critic-free hierarchical optimization. At the trajectory level, it incorporates session-usage signals into advantage estimation. At the session level, it shapes each session’s advantage according to the estimated marginal contribution. Experiments on BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B show that Mosaic outperforms broadcasting in both context compaction and subagent forking scenarios while using fewer sessions on average. Further analyses show that our method achieves improvements in session utility and allocation, which we suggested is a promising target for future advances in multi-session agentic RL.

paper.title: Lean4AgenticRL: Advancing Agentic RL with Verifiable Multi-level Process Rewards

paper.abstract: Abstract Enhancing the agentic capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to tackle complex software engineering (SWE) and general terminal-usage problems is a pressing challenge. Current state-of-the-art LLMs often go through large-scale agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, they mostly rely on high-level outcome rewards ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) , with minimal consideration of low-level toolcall and mid-level workflow-stage rewards, which makes the training less effective. To overcome this limitation, we propose Lean4AgenticRL , which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first framework that grounds multi-level process rewards in the unified Lean4 formalization schema for open-ended agentic RL. Lean4AgenticRL first builds a problem-specific workflow system that balances the agent’s own capability and controllability during execution, laying the foundation for further verification. Subsequently, our workflow formalization and multi-level reward annotation methods enable agent behavior verification within a general harness system. It provides multi-level rewards to support more effective agentic RL with the workflow-stage-normalized GRPO algorithm. Using Lean4AgenticRL , we train LAR-9B/27B , a family of models with enhanced agentic capability. Extensive experiments indicate that our model outperforms the leading model of the similar size. paper.title: Learning from Interaction Experience via Localized Context Distillation
paper.author_block: Zhezheng Hao Yongkang Yang Xilin Xia Jiarui Yu Affiliation: Workbuddy Team, Tencent Yi Liu Affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong Fanjunduo Wei Affiliation: Zhejiang University Peijie Dong Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Tianfu Wang Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Qiang Lin Affiliation: Workbuddy Team, Tencent Can Wang Affiliation: Zhejiang University Hande Dong Jiawei Chen
paper.abstract: Abstract Learning from interaction experience is essential for enabling large language models to continually improve during deployment. Context distillation offers a promising path: privileged information extracted from experience is provided to a teacher, whose behavior is then distilled into a student model that has no access to it. However, both existing forms of context distillation have limitations. Off-policy context distillation trains the student on teacher-generated trajectories and thus suffers from exposure bias; whereas on-policy context distillation trains on the student’s own rollouts, whose states are often uninformative and fail to convey behaviors the student cannot yet produce. To resolve this dilemma, we introduce Localized Context Distillation (LoCD) . LoCD first localizes the critical spans of a student trajectory that require revision. The teacher then regenerates only these spans from the student’s own prefix, and the student is trained on the regenerated segments. LoCD thereby concentrates learning on the most informative states while keeping exposure bias low. Extensive experiments across math reasoning, code generation, and agent tasks demonstrate that LoCD consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves more stable training with smaller and sparser parameter updates. 3 3 footnotetext: Code is available at https://github.com/zz-haooo/LoCD .

Abstract Scaling the training of Large Language Model (LLM) agents typically requires a large collection of executable environments, whose construction, maintenance, and operation constrain the expansion of training experience. Existing offline trajectories offer an opportunity to reuse interaction experience, yet effectively refining the current policy without revisiting these environments remains challenging: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can lead to catastrophic forgetting, while online reinforcement learning requires real-time interaction with the environment. To address this challenge, we propose S tep- A dvantage P olicy D istillation (SAPD), a method for learning from offline trajectories using relative step advantages. SAPD decomposes multi-turn trajectories into individual decision contexts for on-policy distillation, allowing the student to generate responses conditioned on recorded histories, and introduces relative step advantage signals to stabilize training. The entire process requires neither new environment observations nor additional multi-turn interactions. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-based QA show that SAPD improves performance across different teacher configurations, mitigates catastrophic forgetting compared with SFT, and runs at least 4.7 × 4.7\times faster per training step than online OPD.
We will release our code soon.
